title: South Asia
tagline: India’s relations with its neighbours: Pakistan from the 1965 war to Kargil, Bangladesh over water and migration, and China from Panchsheel to the 1962 war.

overview.intro: India is the largest state in South Asia and shares borders, rivers and histories with all of its neighbours, which makes its bilateral relations the organising fact of the region. This unit examines three relationships in structured periods — Pakistan from the 1965 war to Kargil, Bangladesh over the questions of water and migration, and China from the Panchsheel agreement to the war of 1962 — and asks what each dispute reveals about the difficulties of neighbouring states with unequal size.

learn.title: India and Pakistan: from 1965 to Kargil

blocks.text: The relationship between India and Pakistan has been shaped by partition, by Kashmir and by the rivalry that both produce. The war of 1965, fought over Kashmir and the Rann of Kutch, ended in the Tashkent declaration of January 1966 with a return to the pre-war positions mediated by the Soviet Union. The war of 1971 was fought over a different question entirely — the crisis in East Pakistan and the flight of refugees into India — and ended with the creation of Bangladesh, which changed the balance of the subcontinent permanently. The Simla agreement of 1972 converted the ceasefire line in Kashmir into the line of control and undertook to settle differences by bilateral negotiation, which remains the framework’s central provision.

The subsequent decades alternated between negotiation and confrontation. Both states tested nuclear devices in 1998, which raised the stakes of every crisis; the summit of Lahore in 1999 briefly raised hopes; and within weeks the Kargil conflict began when intruders occupied positions across the line of control in the sector that India recovered after fighting in mid-1999. The episode established a pattern that recurs in the relationship: a diplomatic opening is followed by a military probe, the international community calls for restraint and de-escalation, and the underlying questions of Kashmir, cross-border militancy and nuclear thresholds remain unresolved. The structural difficulty is that the two states differ greatly in size yet treat each other as existential rivals, so every issue is read through the security lens before it is discussed on its merits.

learn.title: India and Bangladesh: water and migration

blocks.text: The two permanent questions of the relationship are water and migration, both of which are structural rather than incidental. The Ganges passes through India into Bangladesh, and the Farakka barrage, commissioned upstream in 1975 to meet Calcutta’s dry-season needs, reduced the dry-season flow reaching Bangladesh and produced two decades of protest and intermittent negotiation. The question was settled for a quarter of a century by the agreement of 1996, which fixed a dry-season distribution with minimum flows guaranteed at specific points of measurement, though Bangladesh has continued to argue that the shares were fixed in an unusually dry year and that the arrangement must be reviewed against a longer record. The Teesta, a tributary that flows through India’s states before entering Bangladesh, remains unallocated, which leaves the northern districts of Bangladesh dependent on a flow that India controls entirely and that falls sharply in the dry season.

Migration is the second structural question. Movement across the border has been continuous since partition, and the concerns on each side differ: India points to the effect of large-scale migration on wages, services and the demography of its border states, while Bangladesh points to the treatment of its nationals and to the humanitarian consequences of pushbacks and the border fence. Several of the smaller boundary questions were settled by the 2015 land boundary agreement, which exchanged enclaves and resolved an anomaly left by partition, and it demonstrates that technical disputes can be settled when the political will exists. Trade has grown substantially, and connectivity projects have expanded, but both questions remain live, and each is periodically instrumentalised by domestic politics on both sides.

items: The Farakka barrage began the dry-season water dispute on the Ganges.
The 1996 agreement fixed a sharing formula for twenty-five years.
The Teesta remains unallocated, leaving northern Bangladesh dependent on Indian flows.
Migration and the border fence are the security side of the same neighbourhood.
The 2015 enclave exchange shows that technical disputes can be resolved with will.

learn.title: India and China: Panchsheel to the war of 1962

blocks.text: The relations began in optimism. The Panchsheel agreement of 1954, signed during a period of warm rhetoric, set out five principles for relations between the two countries: mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. The principles were invoked constantly in the diplomacy of the decade and became part of the vocabulary of Indian foreign policy. Beneath the rhetoric, however, the border had never been demarcated: the two sides drew the line differently across thousands of kilometres of the Himalayas, in Aksai Chin in the north-east and in the eastern sector where the McMahon line drawn in 1914 had been accepted by India but rejected by China.

Disagreement became confrontation in 1962. Skirmishes through 1961 and 1962 escalated into a full-scale Chinese offensive in October 1962 across both sectors, which ended with a unilateral Chinese ceasefire after advancing deep into the disputed areas. The war was a profound shock to India: it destroyed the assumptions of the non-aligned diplomacy that had preached friendship, exposed weaknesses in military preparation and intelligence, and left the border question open with an added loss of territory and prestige. Normalization was slow — trade and diplomatic contact were rebuilt over decades, border talks have continued through numerous rounds, and agreements to maintain peace along the line of actual control were reached — but the frontier remains undemarcated and periodic standoffs show that the settlement Panchsheel promised has never been achieved.

learn.title: Assessment: the recurring difficulties of South Asian neighbourhood

blocks.text: Across the three relationships the same difficulties recur. Unequal size means the largest state is expected to reassure while it is simultaneously suspected, and its domestic politics — elections, media, coalition pressures — are read abroad as signals of intent. Unsettled borders turn every incident into a constitutional question, since territory is involved and no leader can be seen to concede it. Rivers and migration bind neighbours together in ways neither can refuse: water flows regardless of treaties and people cross regardless of fences, so cooperation is structurally necessary even where trust is absent.

The record also shows that settlement is possible when the political cost of dispute exceeds the cost of agreement. The Simla framework has held the line of control for decades; the 1996 water agreement functioned for its full term; the 2015 enclave exchange settled an anomaly that had lasted since partition; and trade has expanded even between the pairs with the most difficult relationships. The honest assessment is therefore neither optimistic nor fatalistic: South Asia’s disputes are durable because they touch identity, territory and survival, but they are also ordinary interstate questions that yield to negotiation when leaders choose to pay the domestic cost of settlement. An exam answer that lists disputes without noting this pattern of partial settlement gives only half the picture.

questions.prompt: State four recurring difficulties in India’s relations with its neighbours.
questions.answer: Four difficulties are: the asymmetry of size, which makes neighbours suspect the largest state even while relying on it; undemarcated or disputed borders, which turn every incident into a question of territory that no leader can concede; shared rivers, which flow regardless of treaties and make water allocation a permanent negotiation; and migration and demography, which cross borders whatever fences mark them. The rivalry between India and Pakistan over Kashmir and the nuclear dimension of it are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each difficulty must be named with a concrete example from one of the three relationships.

questions.prompt: Explain the two principal issues in India’s relations with Bangladesh.
questions.answer: The first issue is water. The Ganges enters Bangladesh from India, and the Farakka barrage, commissioned upstream in 1975 to meet Calcutta’s dry-season requirements, reduced the flow reaching Bangladesh, which provoked protests for two decades before a twenty-five year sharing agreement of 1996 fixed minimum dry-season flows, though Bangladesh argues the shares were set in a dry year. The Teesta, a tributary, remains unallocated, which leaves northern Bangladesh dependent on a flow entirely controlled by India. The second issue is migration and the border. Movement across the frontier has been continuous since partition, with India concerned about the effect on wages, services and the demography of its border states, and Bangladesh concerned about the treatment of its nationals and the humanitarian effects of the fence and pushbacks. Both issues are structural, since rivers and people move regardless of agreements, though the land boundary agreement of 2015 shows that the technical elements can be settled when the political will exists.
questions.explanation: Two issues must be identified with the specific river, the specific agreement and the migration question.

questions.prompt: Trace the development of India’s relations with Pakistan from the war of 1965 to the Kargil conflict of 1999.
questions.answer: The relations can be traced through five episodes, each of which redefined the terms of the next. The war of 1965 was fought over Kashmir and the Rann of Kutch, and it ended with the Tashkent declaration of January 1966, mediated by the Soviet Union, which restored the pre-war positions and left the underlying dispute untouched. The war of 1971 arose from a different cause — the crisis in East Pakistan and the flight of refugees into India — and its outcome changed the subcontinent permanently with the creation of Bangladesh, which removed the eastern wing of Pakistan and transformed the balance of power. The Simla agreement of 1972, concluded after that conflict, established the framework that has endured: the ceasefire line became the line of control, and both sides undertook to settle their differences by bilateral negotiation without external mediation. The following decades alternated between negotiation and tension, and the nuclear tests of 1998 on both sides raised the stakes of every subsequent crisis, since a conventional skirmish could no longer be assumed to remain conventional. The Lahore summit of 1999 briefly suggested a breakthrough, and within weeks the Kargil conflict began when intruders occupied positions across the line of control, which India recovered through fighting in the summer of 1999. The pattern across the whole period is of a diplomatic opening followed by a military probe, international calls for restraint, and the permanent questions — Kashmir, cross-border militancy and nuclear thresholds — surviving each round. The judgement an answer should reach is that the relationship has been stable enough to avoid general war since 1971 while remaining permanently unresolved, which is a smaller achievement than peace but a larger one than the frequency of crises suggests.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all five episodes in order with outcomes, plus a judgement on the pattern across the period.

questions.prompt: Are South Asia’s disputes primarily about territory and water, or about the difficulty of neighbouring an unequal power? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case that the disputes are material is straightforward and well evidenced. Territory is involved in every durable confrontation: the Kashmir dispute has produced three wars and a line of control rather than a border, the India–China frontier has never been demarcated and the war of 1962 followed from the mismatch of maps, and the enclave question with Bangladesh festered since partition until 2015. Water is equally concrete: the Farakka barrage diverted Ganges flow from Bangladesh, the Teesta remains unallocated, and rivers cross borders regardless of treaties, so allocation is a permanent negotiation with measurable stakes for agriculture and livelihoods. On this reading the disputes would be tractable if the technical questions were addressed — demarcation, hydrological data, treaty revision — and the obstacle is simply political will. The case that the difficulty lies in the asymmetry of neighbourhood is deeper. A largest state cannot reassure neighbours without appearing to dominate them, and its domestic politics — an election campaign, a television debate, a coalition demand — is read in every capital as a statement of intent, so concessions that would be ordinary between equals become evidence of weakness at home. Each neighbour’s foreign policy is therefore partly a referendum on India’s behaviour, while India’s own security perception is shaped by the fact that its longest disputes involve two states that were once one country and a third with which it fought a war within living memory. The material disputes are visible where the asymmetry works through them: the water question with Bangladesh is inseparable from the perception that the upper riparian state can use its position as leverage, and the migration question is inseparable from the sense of demographic threat that domestic politics magnifies. The strongest conclusion is that neither reading alone explains the record. The material disputes explain why agreement is difficult — the stakes are real and continuous — while the asymmetry explains why agreement is dangerous for leaders on both sides, since any concession is read through the security lens before it is assessed on its merits. The evidence for this synthesis is the pattern of partial settlement: technical questions do get resolved when leaders choose to pay the cost, as with the 2015 enclave exchange and the 1996 water agreement, but the questions that carry symbolic weight for national identity — Kashmir and the undemarcated frontier — resist settlement precisely because they are no longer only about the territory in dispute. Marks are awarded for engaging both readings with specific evidence and for showing how the two interact rather than picking one and ignoring the other.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings argued from concrete evidence, the interaction between them demonstrated with an example, and a reasoned conclusion.
